title: Why India’s Cockroach Movement Might Not Collapse Like the Others
author: Marvin Starominski-Uehara
text:
People gather during a protest organized by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, India, demanding accountability over alleged examination irregularities and education reforms, July 19, 2026.
Credit: Arnav Pratap Singh/Shutterstock.com
When Indian Supreme Court Justice Surya Kant compared certain unemployed youth and activists to cockroaches and parasites in May, he gave a generation searching for a shared identity the charge required to build one. Within days that slur became a rallying cry. Millions of young Indians declared “Main Bhi Cockroach” (‘I too am a cockroach’), turned the insult into memes, and launched a political party in the same breath.Some framed this as Prime Minister Narendra Modi misreading the political environment – after all, his own government gave India’s marginalized and unemployed youth the spark they needed to organize. But that top-down classic political framing overlooks emerging leadership theories, the mechanics of peer-to-peer digital communication, and global trends already underway. Gen Z uprisings had toppled or shaken governments in Nepal, Bangladesh, Kenya, and Madagascar over the previous two years. And each one built from the same digital scaffolding comprised of user digital trace creation, reproduction, and platform scalability.[...]
